chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting comfortable and getting online

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Touch screens, mice and keyboards
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tap, swipe, click, scroll and type on a phone or computer.
This lesson builds toward: On a phone or a computer, you will tap, swipe, click, scroll and type, and fix a typing mistake, without help.
On a phone or tablet you use your finger. Tap once to open something. Swipe (slide your finger) to move up, down or sideways. Press and hold to see more choices.
On a computer you use a mouse or touchpad. Move it to move the arrow on the screen. Click the left button once to choose something. Double-click to open some files. Roll the wheel, or slide two fingers on a touchpad, to scroll.
The keyboard types letters. The Shift key makes a capital letter. Backspace deletes the letter before the cursor. Enter moves to a new line or sends a search.
Step by step:
- Phone: tap an app to open it, swipe to scroll, press the home button or swipe up to go back home.
- Computer: move the mouse, click once to choose, scroll with the wheel.
- Keyboard: type your first name, use Shift for the capital letter, use Backspace to fix a mistake.
Words to know:
- Tap: touch the screen once quickly.
- Swipe: slide your finger across the screen.
- Click: press the mouse button once.
- Cursor: the blinking line that shows where your typing will appear.
Try it now: On a phone or computer, open any app or program, scroll down and back up, then type your first name with a capital letter and fix one mistake with Backspace.
You can now tap, swipe, click, scroll and type on a phone or computer.

check.q: What does "swipe" mean on a phone?
options: Slide your finger across the screen
check.why: Swiping is sliding your finger to move up, down or sideways.

check.q: You need a capital letter at the start of your name. Which key do you hold?
check.why: The Shift key makes a capital letter.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Getting online for free or low cost
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find one free place to get online and know about the Lifeline discount.
This lesson builds toward: Where you live, you will find a free place to get online, connect a phone to Wi-Fi and check whether you qualify for Lifeline, naming the place and its hours.
Public libraries offer free computers and free Wi-Fi. Many community centers, job centers and some restaurants do too. Ask the staff how to sign up for a computer and how long you can use it.
Lifeline is a federal program that lowers the monthly cost of phone or internet service for people with low income or who get help such as SNAP or Medicaid. The standard discount is up to $9.25 a month. You apply through getinternet.gov, then contact a phone or internet company that takes part. Amounts and rules can change, so check lifelinesupport.org for the latest.
On public Wi-Fi, do not do banking or type passwords for important accounts if you can avoid it. Never let a shared computer save your password.
Step by step:
- Call or visit your library or community center and ask about free computers and Wi-Fi.
- To connect a phone to Wi-Fi: open Settings, tap Wi-Fi, pick the network and type the password if there is one.
- If money is tight, check whether you qualify for Lifeline at lifelinesupport.org.
Words to know:
- Wi-Fi: a wireless way to connect to the internet.
- Lifeline: a federal program that lowers phone or internet bills for people who qualify.
- Public Wi-Fi: free Wi-Fi shared by many people in a public place.
Official sources:
- Lifeline Support (USAC, under FCC oversight)
Try it now: Find out your nearest library's or community center's hours for free computer use. If you have a phone, connect it to a Wi-Fi network using Settings, then Wi-Fi.
You can now find a free place to get online, connect to Wi-Fi and know where to check for a lower internet bill.

check.q: Besides libraries, where else can you often find free Wi-Fi?
check.why: Many community centers, job centers and some restaurants offer free Wi-Fi.

check.q: You are on free café Wi-Fi. What should you avoid doing?
check.why: On public Wi-Fi, avoid banking and typing important passwords if you can.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Searching the web and spotting trustworthy sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Search for information and decide if a website can be trusted.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you need to look up, you will search the web and choose a trustworthy result, skipping ads and closing pages with pop-ups or prizes.
A search engine such as Google or Bing finds websites for you. Type a few key words, like "Oakland library hours", into the search box and press Enter.
Not every result is trustworthy. Results marked "Sponsored" or "Ad" are paid ads. Official government sites end in .gov. Look for the real name of the place in the web address.
Be careful with sites that have lots of pop-ups, say you won a prize, ask you to download something, or ask for personal information. Close them and go back.
Step by step:
- Open a web browser and type a few key words in the search box.
- Skip results marked Sponsored or Ad.
- Choose a result whose address matches the real organization or ends in .gov.
- Close any page with pop-ups, prizes or download requests.
Words to know:
- Search engine: a website that finds other websites, like Google or Bing.
- Sponsored: a paid ad shown in search results.
- Pop-up: a window that suddenly appears on top of a page.
Try it now: Search for your public library's hours. Pick the result from the library's own website, not an ad, and write down the hours.
You can now search the web and choose a trustworthy website.

check.q: Which web address is most likely the official site for a U.S. government office?
options: One that says you won a prize
check.why: Official U.S. government websites usually end in .gov.

check.q: You search for your clinic's hours. The first result is an ad. What do you do?
options: Skip it and pick the clinic's own website
check.why: Ads are paid results; the clinic's own site is more trustworthy.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Email, passwords and getting help

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Sending an email with an attachment
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and send an email with a photo or file attached.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free email account, you will send an email with a subject, a short message and a photo or file attached, checking the address, message and attachment before you send.
Email lets you send messages and files to anyone with an email address. Free email services include Gmail and Outlook.com. Your library can help you create an account.
An email has four parts: To (the person's email address), Subject (a few words that say what it is about), the message, and attachments (files or photos you add). The paper-clip icon usually means attach.
Before you press Send, check the address is right, read your message once, and make sure the right file is attached.
Step by step:
- Open your email and choose Compose or New message.
- Type the person's address in To.
- Type a short Subject.
- Write a short, polite message.
- Tap or click the paper clip, choose a photo or file, then press Send.
Words to know:
- Email address: an address like name@example.com where you get email.
- Subject: the short title of an email.
- Attachment: a file or photo sent with an email.
Try it now: Send an email to a friend or family member with the subject "Practice email", a one-line message and one photo attached.
You can now write and send an email with an attachment.

check.q: In an email, what goes in the To line?
check.why: The To line holds the email address of the person you are writing to.

check.q: You wrote your email but forgot the photo. What do you do before sending?
options: Click the paper clip and attach the photo
check.why: The paper-clip icon attaches a photo or file before you press Send.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a strong password and keeping accounts safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a strong password and know how to protect your accounts.
This lesson builds toward: When you make or use an account, you will create a strong password and protect your accounts, never sharing a code and signing out of shared computers.
A strong password is long and hard to guess. One easy way: string together three or four random words with a number and a symbol, like "Blue-Taco-River-58". Do not use your name, birthday or "password123".
Use a different password for your email than for other accounts. Your email is the key to resetting everything else.
Turn on two-step verification if your account offers it: after your password, you also enter a code sent to your phone. Never give that code to anyone who calls or texts you, even if they say they are from the company.
Step by step:
- Pick three or four random words.
- Join them and add a number and a symbol.
- Use it only for this account.
- Turn on two-step verification in your account's security settings.
- Never share the code sent to your phone.
Words to know:
- Password: a secret word or phrase that lets only you into an account.
- Two-step verification: a second check, usually a code sent to your phone, after your password.
Try it now: Make up a strong password using three random words, a number and a symbol. Do not use it as written here. Write a hint, not the password, somewhere safe at home.
You can now create a strong password and protect your account with two-step verification.

options: A second check, like a code to your phone
check.why: After your password, you also enter a code sent to your phone.

check.q: You want a password for your new email. Which is best?
options: Three random words joined with a number and a symbol
The same password as your bank
check.why: Long, random words with a number and symbol are hard to guess.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Asking a free AI assistant for tech help
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a free AI assistant to get step-by-step help with a tech problem.
This lesson builds toward: When you are stuck with a tech task, you will ask a free AI assistant for short steps and describe what you see when a step does not match, without typing any password, code or private number.
When you are stuck, a free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can explain how to do something, step by step, in simple words. You can type or talk to it.
Say what device you have and what you want to do. For example: "I have an Android phone. How do I attach a photo to an email in Gmail? Give me short steps." If a step does not match your screen, tell it what you see.
Never type passwords, codes, bank numbers or your Social Security number into an AI. And a library staff member is always a good person to ask too.
Step by step:
- Open a free AI assistant.
- Say your device and what you want to do.
- Ask for short, simple steps.
- If a step does not match, describe what you see on your screen.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: a computer program you chat with in everyday words.
- Device: a phone, tablet or computer.
Try it now: Final task: search for your library's hours on its official site, take a screenshot or photo, and email it to someone with a polite message. If you get stuck, ask an AI assistant for steps. Sign out if you used a shared computer.
You can now get online, find trustworthy information, send it by email and get help safely when you are stuck.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Trustworthy search Used an ad or a site that is not the library's own. Found the hours on the library's official website. Can say how they knew the site was official. Screenshot or photo No screenshot or photo of the hours. A clear screenshot or photo that shows the hours. Took it without help. Email sent Email missing a subject, message or attachment. Sent with a subject, a short polite message and the photo attached. The person confirmed they got it and could see the photo. Account safety Weak password, or did not sign out of a shared computer. Account has a strong password, and signed out of any shared computer. Two-step verification is turned on. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What two things should your first tech-help prompt say?
options: Your device and what you want to do
check.why: The AI needs your device and your goal to give the right steps.

check.q: The AI says to tap "Settings" but you do not see it. What do you do?
options: Type your password to the AI
Tell the AI what you see on your screen
check.why: Describing your screen helps the AI give steps that match.
